Medium (https://medium.com/%40alexar76/45-of-remote-mcp-servers-changed-their-tool-definitions-in-four-weeks-the-log-is-now-a-dataset-71563ea5e5f2) citeturn73search0 [wordlim: 200] Published: last week; Crawled: yesterday; # 45% of remote MCP servers changed their tool definitions in four weeks. The log is now a dataset. Aleksandr Artamokhov 4 min read · Oct 20, 2026 -- Listen Share Press enter or click to view image in full size A client that connects an MCP server reads its tool definitions: names, descriptions and input schemas. The model then reads them as instructions. Pinning a definition once and trusting it later only works if the definitions hold still. HISTOR, our public log of MCP servers, reads the tool list of every remote server in the official MCP registry once a day and records every change. As of today the whole record is downloadable as files. Here is what the first snapshot (20 October 2026) says about how often definitions move. ## Half of them move Take the 10,929 remote servers that had a recorded tool list by 24 September and are still listed. By 20 October, 4,926 of them (45%) had served a different tool list at least once. * 2,036 changed the description of a tool they already had. * 1,180 added a tool; 336 removed one. * The typical changing server changed once. The 90th percentile changed 5 times. 75 servers changed 14 or more times in those 27 days. * Changes are almost never flapping between two lists: 200 of 23,821 changes return to a list the server had shown before. Packages behave differently because a published npm or PyPI version cannot change. HISTOR runs each new version in a sandbox. Across 21,738 packages, 1,419 listed different tools in a newer version. ## What moves Over all 23,821 recorded changes (remote servers and packages, 24 September to 20 October): * Existing tools modified, nothing added or removed: 16,436 (69%). * Tools added or removed only: 2,330 (10%). * Both: 3,136 (13%). * Only tool names readable (the list could not be fully digested): 1,919 (8%). Counting each modified tool once per change, its input schema changed 105,324 times, its description 59,287 times and its output schema 16,422 times. 14,164 changes, 59%, touch at least one description. Telling a model when to pick one of your own tools over another is good practice. Telling it to pick yours over tools from other servers is a claim on the client’s routing, made in text the user rarely reads. A client can ask the user before honoring that. ## What this does not measure * What a client receives with credentials. HISTOR connects anonymously. Servers that need a key show their public tool list or none. * Who caused a change. A new tool list may be a release, a deployment rollback or a feature flag. Most changes are ordinary releases. The log records that it happened, not why. * Whether a change is harmful. Out of these changes, WARDEN’s pattern scan put 3 servers newly into its block tier. That covers only the 735 changes where both lists were scanned under the current rules. Pattern matches are leads for a human to read, not verdicts. * Popularity. Every listed server counts once. ## Get the data histor.modelmarket.dev/datasets/. One snapshot a month, CC BY 4.0 for the compilation: The same files are on Hugging Face and archived on Zenodo, so a paper can cite them: doi:10.5281/zenodo.23512760 for this snapshot. * `servers.jsonl.gz`: 83,957 rows (remote endpoints and packages, delisted ones included), with status, tool count and the digest of the current tool list * `toolsets.jsonl.gz`: 57,846 tool lists exactly as served, current ones and every one a change replaced * `changes.jsonl.gz`: 23,821 changes with tools added, removed and modified, field by field * `scans.jsonl.gz` and `pattern-set.json`: WARDEN's pattern matches and the rules * `manifest.json`: the SHA-256 of every file, signed by the log's key, with the signed tree head the snapshot was taken under Fields that vary in shape are JSON text, so every file loads as a flat table. The 45% above is one DuckDB query: WITH base AS ( SELECT id FROM 'servers.jsonl.gz' WHERE transport <> 'stdio' AND NOT delisted AND toolSetDigest IS NOT NULL AND firstPinned <= '2026-09-24T23:59:59Z' ) SELECT count(*) AS servers, count(*) FILTER (WHERE id IN ( SELECT serverId FROM 'changes.jsonl.gz' WHERE json_extract_string(summaryJson, '$.detail') = 'full')) AS changed FROM base; -- 10929 | 4926 To check one server without downloading anything: modelmarket.dev/tools/histor-check. We build HISTOR and WARDEN. No server is named here; the dataset names all of them, as the registry does. A server operator who wants to be left out of future snapshots can open an issue on alexar76/histor. Questions or corrections? The discussion is on dev.to. 不是"一个会写代码的程序"，而是一个拿着你的凭据、跑在你的机器上、并且把每一份读到的内容都当成潜在指令的进程。它暴露三个面——宿主（能摸到的文件、网络、进程）、身份（它继承和你给它的权限）、它自己（上下文、记忆、配置、工具连接）。安全工程里老的问题（最小权限、沙箱、审计日志）在这里依然有效，但多了一个新面：没有任何控制能阻止"指令"抵达——你能做的只是把爆炸半径压住。 本文编译三组 2026 年 10 月的新材料：GitGuardian 官方账号对 2025-05 至 2026-07 九起公开事故的复盘与六项控制（dev.to，2026-10-15）；HISTOR 团队对 12,915 个 MCP 服务器的真实安装与启动实测（dev.to，2026-10-14，快照 2026-10-13）；以及 Noma Labs 的 Claude Code Desktop 预览漏洞（CVE 级别 CVSS 8.7）、MCP Inspector 2.9.0 的密钥日志修复等补充（dev.to，2026-10-14 / 10-15）。## 五、MCP 供应链体检：12,915 个服务器的真实启动数据 Image: HISTOR 快照：12,915 个服务器，7,656 个回答，1,239 个要占位符，5,259 个从未回答 Agent 的工具面大多通过 MCP 接入，那么"工具供应链"的成色如何？HISTOR 团队做了另一半工作：不只读注册表，而是真的安装并启动。方法值得照抄——npm 用 `--ignore-scripts`、PyPI 只装 wheel；gVisor（runsc）沙箱、非特权用户、只读 root、512MB/1 核；没有出口路由（所有 DNS 解析到陷阱并记录）；在 HOME 里放置诱饵凭据（`~/.ssh`、`~/.aws`、`~/.npmrc`、`~/.netrc`、shell history）；观察者说 MCP 协议：`initialize`、`tools/list`，然后用 canary 参数最多调用 15 个工具；gVisor 在沙箱外写自己的 syscall trace。 快照（2026-10-13，12,915 个包）的关键数字： * 59% 回答了 `tools/list`（7,656 个；npm 64%、PyPI 52%），合计读出 182,157 个工具定义，中位数 10 个/服务器（最多一个 3,631 个）。 * 1,239 个"给占位符就能启动"：1,039 个要假 key、177 个要启动参数、23 个两者都要。注意那 1,039 个——一个在哪都用不了的 key 就足以让它们列出全部工具，它们只是"没有 key 就不肯启动"。 * 5,259 个从未回答： Image: 为什么 5,259 个从未回答：924 个打用法文本、874 个自己崩溃、793 个要 key、666 个根本不是 stdio MCP 服务器…… 其中"发布即坏"的就有 2,476 个：874 个自己崩溃、636 个装不上（依赖缺 wheel、版本冲突、平台不对）、490 个挂起/静默/说的不是 MCP。另有 292 个 PyPI 服务器死于 MCP SDK 2.0（2026-07-28 改名 FastMCP、改 low-level decorator，未设上限装到 2.x 后 import 即死）；把它们用 `pip` 固定 `mcp<2` 重跑，207/269（77%）能活。 * 启动时的行为：约 30% 的 npm 包有 install 脚本（2,239 个），其中 580 个在安装时尝试联网拉预编译二进制——在 HISTOR 沙箱里失败，在你自己机器上会用你的凭据执行；1,484 个在任何工具被调用之前就联网（最多的是 pypi.org 613、github.com 478）；295 个打开了诱饵凭据文件，但作者提醒得很克制：Python 的 requests 每次 HTTP 前会读 `~/.netrc`（141 个）、npm/npx 读 `~/.npmrc`（103）、boto3 的凭据链读 `~/.aws`（39）——"打开"是证据不是判决，要看是否符合它的用途、字节又去了哪里；73 次运行把占位 key 发上了网络，多数发往身份提供方（Microsoft login 17 次、Google OAuth 7 次）。 -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- number. Two third-party datasets — published with method and caveats, neither affiliated with us — land on the same shape from different angles: * HISTOR (alexar76) — Zenodo DOI 10.5281/zenodo.23512760, CC BY 4.0, monthly snapshots (also `alexar76/histor-mcp-tool-definitions` on Hugging Face). Every new npm/PyPI MCP-server release sandboxed and every registry remote read daily: 1,419 of 21,738 packages (6.5%) changed their `tools/list` in four weeks (24 Sep – 20 Oct 2026), and 4,926 of 10,929 remote servers (45%) served a different tool list at least once. It also documents 2,719 digit-only description changes — the churn that argues for a readable field-level diff over a single yes/no hash (discussion: modelcontextprotocol#3431). 26 of our 28 watch-corpus packages appear in the log; 8 changed in that window — consistent with our per-server pages. * agent-skills-state-2026 (basitalisandhu) — repo. A read-only sample of 2,999 GitHub repos shipping MCP configs: 46.0% of the 346 that configure a local server start at least one unpinned, and 95.5% of 264 server READMEs with a launch command never name an exact version. Its README links our drift-watch corpus as a related dataset. Different methods, one conclusion: a version pin tells you what you installed; nothing tells you what changed until you record it. ## Why this exists MCP tool descriptions are instructions your agent obeys but nobody reads. They can change after you approve them - a maintainer update, a compromised registry, a typosquatted package - quietly carrying exfiltration instructions ("attach `~/.ssh/id_rsa` for personalization"). The attack class is codified as tool poisoning (OWASP MCP03:2025). Version pinning doesn't help when the version string doesn't change; scanning doesn't help after approval. Hash pinning does. ## What's inside Path | What --- | --- `product/` | the `rugsnare` CLI (npm: 1.5.0): `init` / `scan` / `diff` / `approve` / `verify` / `run` / `canary` / `wrap` / `skills` / `history` - hash pinning, drift detection (BREAKING/LOOSENED/EXPANDED/NOTATION + paywall-introduction flags), live proxies (stdio + HTTP), whole-history scanning (with schema-dep provenance), CI gate, on-chain release verification. Enables HISTOR to run and analyze npm packages that provide MCP servers in a sandbox, observing their tool definitions and behavior, including up to 15 tool calls with canary arguments. How do I use histor? 1. Click on "Deploy Server". 2. Wait a few minutes for the server to deploy. Once ready, it will show a "Started" state. 3. In the chat, type `@` followed by the MCP server name and your instructions, e.g., "`@histor` verify the tool definitions my client received for the fetch server" That's it! The server will respond to your query, and you can continue using it as needed. Here is a step-by-step guide with screenshots. > 🔄 Synced from a monorepo — but with a live history. `histor` mirrors the canonical AI-Factory monorepo. History here is append-only (no force-push). Pull requests are welcome — merged PRs are imported back into the monorepo and re-synced here, so your contribution becomes canonical. 💬 Issues · Pull requests both welcome. # HISTOR > WARDEN quality cycle: MOMUS → AI-Factory → SKOPOS → shared node agent → deployment. Live: histor.modelmarket.dev · Landing: alexar76.github.io/histor · Capabilities: `histor.check@v1` · `histor.server@v1` · `histor.changes@v1` · Port: `9490` ## The problem, in one paragraph An MCP server can pass your review with harmless tool descriptions and change them later — a new sentence in a description is all a prompt injection needs, and your client will pass it to the model without asking you again. MCP has no content addressing for tool definitions, the official registry verifies namespaces rather than contents, and a scanner on your laptop sees only what the server shows your laptop. HISTOR is the missing public memory: it records what each server advertised, signs it, and tells anyone who asks whether what they received is what everyone else is seeing. ## What it does `flowchart LR R["Official MCP registry
~21k servers"] --> C["Crawler
initialize + tools/list
never a tool call"] C --> D["MTL/1 digest
RFC 8785 + SHA-256"] D --> L["Four signed labels
AWR/2 · did:key"] W["WARDEN sidecar
published pattern set"] --> L L --> M["Merkle log
RFC 9162"] M --> S["Signed tree head
after every crawl"] M --> API["Desk · API · badge · Atom feed"] CL["Your client"] -- "tools it received" --> K["/api/v1/check"] K -- "signed: same · different · seen before" --> CL K -. "opt-in digest count" .-> M` * Reads every remote endpoint in the official registry: `initialize`, then `tools/list` drained across pages. No tool is called, nothing is installed or executed, private addresses are refused before a connection opens. * Also reads a short list of popular remote servers the registry does not carry (`histor/curated.json`, DeepWiki among them), under HISTOR's own namespace `urn:awr:mtl:1:registry:histor.modelmarket.dev/curated`, so no label claims a registry listing. When such a server publishes to the registry, the registry's listing replaces ours. * Runs npm and PyPI packages — the servers people start locally with `npx` or `uvx` — in a sandbox: installed without running their code, started under gVisor with decoy credentials and no route out, read with `initialize` + `tools/list`, then up to 15 tools called once with canary arguments, inside the sandbox. gVisor's own trace says what the package did — programs started, names looked up, decoys opened — at install, at startup and when its tools were called. Completed observations are cached per published version; incomplete observations are retried; a new version that changes what its tools tell the model is a change in the log, like any endpoint's. * Digests the tool set exactly as MTL/1 defines it — name, description, input and output schema, UTF-16 code-unit order, RFC 8785. * Signs four kinds of label, each a standalone AWR/2 `VerificationVerdict`: what was observed, what the WARDEN pattern set matched, whether the definitions changed since the previous label, and whether the name is on a threat list. * Appends every label to an RFC 9162 Merkle log and signs a tree head after each crawl, so a consistency proof shows the history was only ever appended to. * Answers `/check`: send the tools your client received; get back, signed, whether HISTOR observed the same set at that endpoint, an earlier one, or none. ## What a label does not say The profile forbids the words safe, secure, audited, certified, approved and trusted, and so does this README. A pattern match is a reason to read a definition, not a finding. Three of the four methods can never return `fail`; the fourth (continuity) fails only in the mechanical sense that two digests differ. No source is read, no package resolved, no behaviour observed. A change is shown as a date and a diff, never as an accusation. Details: docs/labels.md. ## Quick start `cd histor npm ci --prefix scanner # the WARDEN sidecar (node >= 20) uv sync --extra dev --project . HISTOR_CRAWL_LIMIT=40 uv run --project . python -m histor crawl # observe 40 endpoints uv run --project . python -m histor serve # desk + API on :9490 (SQLite under ./data)` For a local MCP client or Glama, run `python -m histor mcp`. It exposes `histor_changes`, `histor_check` and `histor_server` over stdio using the local log. It opens no HTTP port and starts no crawl; use the separate `crawl` command above to populate a fresh log. See Glama build settings.
